Chapter Six: The Aftermath of Escape—Navigating a New World.
Imagine stepping into freedom after a lifetime behind walls. For someone who’d spent years under constant watch, every open street, every unguarded conversation—they felt almost unreal. The world outside North Korea was dazzling, but also deeply disorienting.
Freedom, it turned out, wasn’t a single, soaring moment. It was a series of tiny, uncertain steps. At first, even the simplest things could be overwhelming. Think about walking into a supermarket with endless rows of food, or seeing strangers smile without any suspicion. Silence where once there’d been blaring propaganda. Each of these things was a reminder—not just of what had been lost, but of how much there was to relearn.
He moved carefully through his new life, always half-expecting the rules to change, or for the ground to suddenly shift beneath him. And he wasn’t alone. He met others who’d made the same journey, each carrying their own scars and stories. Some managed to adapt, slowly building new families and routines. But others struggled, haunted by memories that wouldn’t let go, or unable to trust even the simplest acts of kindness.
That’s when he realized—escaping North Korea wasn’t the end of suffering. It was really just the start of a different kind of struggle.
Finding work was tough. The skills that had helped him survive back home—being watchful, staying silent, obeying without question—didn’t really translate to this new world. Here, people valued openness and taking initiative. So he took whatever jobs he could, learning new routines, trying to fit in. Sometimes, he’d catch himself pausing before he spoke, like he was still waiting for permission. Those old habits, shaped by years of fear, were stubborn and slow to fade.
And then there was the loneliness. He missed his family, especially his mother. Her absence was a wound that never quite healed. He wrote letters he could never send, replayed old memories—some comforting, others painful. That feeling of being an outsider, first in Japan, then in North Korea, now followed him into this new life.
Yet, in the midst of all this, there were moments of hope. A neighbor who invited him in for a meal. A coworker who listened without judging. The laughter of a child in the park. These small acts of kindness reminded him that healing wasn’t just possible—it was real.
Slowly, he began to see that freedom isn’t just the absence of chains. It’s the presence of connection, of possibility.
Over time, he learned how to find his way in this new world. He found ways to honor his past without letting it trap him. He built relationships, this time grounded in trust instead of fear. The journey was slow and sometimes painful, but it was also filled with moments of grace.
He came to understand something important: survival isn’t only about endurance. It’s about learning how to truly live again.
